text:
The three days of travel in Genesis 22 have the nature of a suspended sentence; during them nothing outward happens, and yet everything of significance happens. The servants are specified, and the wood, the knife, and the fire; the instruments of the act are thus named before the act itself occurs. Obedience and horror remain together in the story, and neither prevails over the other. Faith, in such an account, has the form of an ordered relation or arrangement; it is not rendered as a feeling.

Compared with the earlier promise, the scene seems less remote from it than at first it might appear. Isaac is recalled as the child of the covenant, the one through whom the nations are to be blessed; and the covenant promise becomes a test. The scene depends on one word, hineni, "here I am," spoken by Abraham three times, to God, to Isaac, and to the angel. In each place the word has another value; in each succeeding place it costs him more. The language of being present is also, in this story, the language of loss.
